answer:
In short: tracing records what your agent or app did. Evaluations score your app's behaviour so you can compare versions, and their results can be linked back to the agent's traces. Signals automatically score and tag your agent's conversations in production.

**Tracing: records what happened**
- With the Weave SDK for Agents, each turn, LLM call and tool call is recorded as a span, which is a structured record of one operation. Spans are grouped into conversations in the **Agents** tab [S6]. The stated purpose is to let you "view, debug, and evaluate" your agent's behaviour [S6].
- For non-agent LLM code, integrations record calls as Weave **Calls** in the **Traces** view [S3]. A Trace is a full tree of Calls that share the same execution context [S7].

**Evaluations: measuring quality**
- An `Evaluation` brings together a dataset of test examples and one or more scoring functions. Each `.evaluate()` creates an evaluation run [S2].
- Use evaluations to compare changes over time and catch regressions [S2].

**Signals: monitoring agents in production**
- The Signals tab in the Agents view shows tags and ratings for your agent's conversations. It points out quality and safety problems and highlights the traces that need your attention [S1].
- A rating is a score between 0.0 and 1.0, and a tag is a label such as "user-frustration". Both are attached to matching spans [S4].

**How they fit together**
- **Tracing and evaluations:** Weave's agent-evaluation tutorial traces an agent as a conversation, scores its runs, and compares versions, "all linked back to the agent transcripts" [S9]. That way, evaluation results stay connected to the traced behaviour behind them.
- **Tracing and Signals:** Signals score the conversations and spans that tracing has captured [S1][S4].
- **Choose the current approach:** The older Monitors page says it covers "a previous approach" and recommends Signals under Weave for Agents for new implementations [S8].

In short: tracing records what your application or agent did. Evaluations measure your application against a fixed, curated set of test cases. Signals score and tag the traced conversations of your live agents. The last two both rely on getting your app's activity into Weave.

**Tracing: records what happened**
- If you build agents with the Weave SDK for Agents, Weave records conversations, turns, LLM calls and tool calls as structured records called spans. You can view them in the **Agents** tab [S6]. The stated purpose is to let you "view, debug, and evaluate" your agent's behaviour [S6].
- For non-agent LLM code, integrations record individual calls as Weave **Calls** in the **Traces** view [S3]. A Trace is a full tree of Calls that share the same execution context [S7].

**Evaluations: testing before you ship**
- An `Evaluation` brings together a dataset of test examples and one or more scoring functions [S2].
- You run it against a `Model` or a function containing your app's logic. Each `.evaluate()` creates an evaluation run [S2]. In TypeScript, the target is any function wrapped with `weave.op` [S2].
- Use evaluations to compare changes over time and catch regressions [S2].

**Signals: monitoring agents in production**
- In the Agents view, the Signals tab shows tags and ratings for your agent's conversations [S1].
- A rating is a score between 0.0 and 1.0, and a tag is a label such as "user-frustration". Both are attached to matching spans [S4].
- Signals point out quality and safety problems and highlight the traces that need your attention [S1].

**How they fit together**
- Tracing is the foundation. Evaluations check changes against repeatable test cases [S2]. Signals keep scoring real agent conversations in production [S1].
- Putting these premises together: a Signal can flag a weak trace, and that can guide what you test next in an evaluation. The pages I read don't describe this as an official workflow.
- Note: Signals belong to the newer Agents workflow. They replace the older Monitors approach, so don't mix the two.

# Trace your agents

> Use the Weave SDK to instrument multi-turn agentic applications and view them in the Agents tab.

> [!TIP]
>
> **This workflow is also available in CoreWeave Agent Lens.** Agent Lens is the Forge experience built for tracing, monitoring, and analyzing AI agents, with automated insights into agent failures and user intents. It uses the same trace data as Weights & Biases Weave, so the traces you already send appear there with nothing to migrate.
> [See how to do this in Agent Lens](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/agent-lens/tracing/instrument.md).

Learn how to instrument a multi-turn agentic application using the W\&B Weave SDK so that you can view, debug, and evaluate your agent's behavior. This guide is intended for developers who build or integrate agents and want structured visibility into conversations, turns, LLM calls, and tool executions.

The Weave SDK for Agents models the full lifecycle of a multi-turn agent conversation: the agent that owns many conversations, the conversation that groups turns together, each user-agent exchange (turn), the LLM calls within a turn, and the tool executions that an LLM triggers. Traces appear in the **Agents** tab of your Weave project. Each conversation shows a multi-turn timeline with nested tool calls, token usage, and feedback.

Weave is built on [OpenTelemetry (OTel)](https://opentelemetry.io/docs/concepts/), the open standard for distributed tracing. Every turn, LLM call, and tool call emits an OTel *span* (a structured record of one operation). Each span is tagged with [GenAI semantic-convention](https://opentelemetry.io/docs/specs/semconv/gen-ai/) attributes like `gen_ai.agent.name` and `gen_ai.conversation.id`.

If you're tracing individual functions as Ops with the `@weave.op` decorator, see [Trace LLM applications](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/tracking/tracing.md) instead.

# Integrations overview

> Trace agents and LLM applications with Weave's integrations for agent SDKs, harnesses, LLM providers, and orchestration frameworks.

Weave provides two ways to integrate with your AI stack:

* **Trace agents**: for multi-turn agentic applications built with agent SDKs (such as the OpenAI Agents SDK or Google ADK) or run inside agent harnesses (such as Claude Code, Codex, or Pi.dev). These integrations capture sessions, turns, LLM calls, and tool calls, and render them in the Weave **Agents** view.
* **Trace LLM applications**: for code that calls LLM providers (OpenAI, Anthropic, Bedrock, and others) or uses orchestration frameworks (LangChain, LlamaIndex, DSPy, and others). These integrations capture individual LLM calls and pipeline steps as Weave **Calls** in the **Traces** view.

If you're not sure which path to take, start with [Trace your agents](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/tracking/trace-agents.md) for new multi-turn agent work, or [Trace LLM applications](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/tracking/tracing.md) for existing LLM-call workflows.

## Traces

Traces are full trees of Calls that share the same execution context. Each Trace contains an ID (`trace_id`) you can use to retrieve the entire tree of Calls. If you retrieve Call information using the Call's ID, Weave returns data about the specified Call only, and none of its child Calls.

# Evaluations overview

> Evaluation-driven LLM application development to systematically improve applications

*Evaluation-driven LLM application development* helps you systematically improve LLM applications by measuring their behavior using consistent, curated examples.

This guide shows you how to set up and run evaluations in Weave so you can measure your LLM application's performance against repeatable test cases, compare changes over time, and identify regressions. It's intended for developers building LLM applications who want to move beyond ad hoc testing into a structured, measurable workflow.

**Python**

In Weave, the core of the workflow is the *`Evaluation` object*, which defines:

* A [`Dataset`](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/core-types/datasets) or list of dictionaries for test examples.
* One or more [scoring functions](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/evaluation/scorers.md).
* Optional configuration like [input preprocessing](#format-dataset-rows-before-evaluating).

Once you've defined the `Evaluation`, you can run it against a [`Model`](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/core-types/models) object or any custom function containing LLM application logic. Each call to `.evaluate()` triggers an *evaluation run*. Think of the `Evaluation` object as a blueprint, and each run as a measurement of how your application performs under that setup.

**TypeScript**

In Weave, the core of the workflow is the *`Evaluation` object*, which defines:

* A [`Dataset`](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/core-types/datasets) or array of objects for test examples.
* One or more [scoring functions](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/evaluation/scorers.md).

Once you've defined the `Evaluation`, you can run it against any function wrapped with `weave.op`. Each call to `.evaluate()` triggers an *evaluation run*. Think of the `Evaluation` object as a blueprint, and each run as a measurement of how your application performs under that setup.

> [!NOTE]
>
> The TypeScript SDK uses function-based models and scorers. Class-based `Model` and `Scorer` types are not yet available in TypeScript.

To get started with evaluations, complete the following steps:

1. [Create an `Evaluation` object](#create-an-evaluation-object)

# Monitor using built-in signals

> Weights & Biases provides built-in scoring solutions for agents in production

> [!NOTE]
>
> This page covers a previous approach to monitoring production traffic. For new implementations, use **Signals** under Weave for Agents. See [View agent signals](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/tracking/view-agent-signals.md).

Standard system metrics like latency, token count, and cost don't fully capture agent behavior. Inspecting individual traces provides deep insight but doesn't scale to the millions of traces generated in a live environment.

Signals provide a high-level monitoring solution to this problem by offering automated, behavioral scoring for agents in production:

* Automated scoring: Every incoming production trace is automatically processed and scored on common quality issues and errors.
* Infrastructure: Processing is powered by CoreWeave compute and CoreWeave GPUs for scalability across millions of traces.

By using signals within production, you can:

* Gain behavioral insight. Move beyond system metrics to understand if your agent is hallucinating, failing to follow conversation patterns, or losing grounding in its evidence.
* Accelerate the research loop. Use the scores and failure analyses generated by signals to identify weaknesses, which you can use to research model improvement, data annotation, or reinforcement learning.

# Integrations overview

> Trace agents and LLM applications with Weave's integrations for agent SDKs, harnesses, LLM providers, and orchestration frameworks.

Weave provides two ways to integrate with your AI stack:

* **Trace agents**: for multi-turn agentic applications built with agent SDKs (such as the OpenAI Agents SDK or Google ADK) or run inside agent harnesses (such as Claude Code, Codex, or Pi.dev). These integrations capture sessions, turns, LLM calls, and tool calls, and render them in the Weave **Agents** view.
* **Trace LLM applications**: for code that calls LLM providers (OpenAI, Anthropic, Bedrock, and others) or uses orchestration frameworks (LangChain, LlamaIndex, DSPy, and others). These integrations capture individual LLM calls and pipeline steps as Weave **Calls** in the **Traces** view.

If you're not sure which path to take, start with [Trace your agents](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/tracking/trace-agents.md) for new multi-turn agent work, or [Trace LLM applications](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/tracking/tracing.md) for existing LLM-call workflows.

Learn how to instrument a multi-turn agentic application using the W\&B Weave SDK so that you can view, debug, and evaluate your agent's behavior. This guide is intended for developers who build or integrate agents and want structured visibility into conversations, turns, LLM calls, and tool executions.

The Weave SDK for Agents models the full lifecycle of a multi-turn agent conversation: the agent that owns many conversations, the conversation that groups turns together, each user-agent exchange (turn), the LLM calls within a turn, and the tool executions that an LLM triggers. Traces appear in the **Agents** tab of your Weave project. Each conversation shows a multi-turn timeline with nested tool calls, token usage, and feedback.

Weave is built on [OpenTelemetry (OTel)](https://opentelemetry.io/docs/concepts/), the open standard for distributed tracing. Every turn, LLM call, and tool call emits an OTel *span* (a structured record of one operation). Each span is tagged with [GenAI semantic-convention](https://opentelemetry.io/docs/specs/semconv/gen-ai/) attributes like `gen_ai.agent.name` and `gen_ai.conversation.id`.

If you're tracing individual functions as Ops with the `@weave.op` decorator, see [Trace LLM applications](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/tracking/tracing.md) instead.

> Weights & Biases provides built-in scoring solutions for agents in production

Standard system metrics like latency, token count, and cost don't fully capture agent behavior. Inspecting individual traces provides deep insight but doesn't scale to the millions of traces generated in a live environment.

Signals provide a high-level monitoring solution to this problem by offering automated, behavioral scoring for agents in production:

* Automated scoring: Every incoming production trace is automatically processed and scored on common quality issues and errors.
* Infrastructure: Processing is powered by CoreWeave compute and CoreWeave GPUs for scalability across millions of traces.

By using signals within production, you can:

* Gain behavioral insight. Move beyond system metrics to understand if your agent is hallucinating, failing to follow conversation patterns, or losing grounding in its evidence.
* Accelerate the research loop. Use the scores and failure analyses generated by signals to identify weaknesses, which you can use to research model improvement, data annotation, or reinforcement learning.

## What gets traced

After you run an agent with the exporter enabled, Koog forwards traces to your Weave project. Koog's Weave exporter captures the same spans as Koog's general OTEL integration, including:

* Agent lifecycle events (start, stop, errors)
* LLM interactions (prompts, completions, token usage, latency)
* Tool and API calls (function calls and external requests)

> Evaluate AI outputs and return evaluation metrics with Weave Scorers

In Weave, Scorers evaluate AI outputs and return evaluation metrics. They take the AI's output, analyze it, and return a dictionary of results. Scorers can use your input data as reference if needed and can also output extra information, such as explanations or reasoning from the evaluation.

# Evaluations overview

> Evaluation-driven LLM application development to systematically improve applications

*Evaluation-driven LLM application development* helps you systematically improve LLM applications by measuring their behavior using consistent, curated examples.

This guide shows you how to set up and run evaluations in Weave so you can measure your LLM application's performance against repeatable test cases, compare changes over time, and identify regressions. It's intended for developers building LLM applications who want to move beyond ad hoc testing into a structured, measurable workflow.

**Python**

In Weave, the core of the workflow is the *`Evaluation` object*, which defines:

* A [`Dataset`](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/core-types/datasets) or list of dictionaries for test examples.
* One or more [scoring functions](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/evaluation/scorers.md).
* Optional configuration like [input preprocessing](#format-dataset-rows-before-evaluating).

Once you've defined the `Evaluation`, you can run it against a [`Model`](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/core-types/models) object or any custom function containing LLM application logic. Each call to `.evaluate()` triggers an *evaluation run*. Think of the `Evaluation` object as a blueprint, and each run as a measurement of how your application performs under that setup.

**TypeScript**

In Weave, the core of the workflow is the *`Evaluation` object*, which defines:

* A [`Dataset`](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/core-types/datasets) or array of objects for test examples.
* One or more [scoring functions](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/evaluation/scorers.md).

Once you've defined the `Evaluation`, you can run it against any function wrapped with `weave.op`. Each call to `.evaluate()` triggers an *evaluation run*. Think of the `Evaluation` object as a blueprint, and each run as a measurement of how your application performs under that setup.

> [!NOTE]
>
> The TypeScript SDK uses function-based models and scorers. Class-based `Model` and `Scorer` types are not yet available in TypeScript.

To get started with evaluations, complete the following steps:

1. [Create an `Evaluation` object](#create-an-evaluation-object)
2. [Define a dataset of examples](#define-a-dataset-of-test-examples)
3. [Define scoring functions](#define-scoring-functions)
4. [Define a model or function to evaluate](#define-a-model-or-function-to-evaluate)
5. [Run the evaluation](#run-the-evaluation)

After completing these steps, you'll have a reusable evaluation configuration and an evaluation run whose results you can inspect in the Weights & Biases UI. For a complete evaluation code sample, see the [full evaluation code example](#full-evaluation-code-example). You can also learn more about [advanced evaluation features](#advanced-evaluation-usage) like [Saved views](#saved-views) and [Imperative evaluations](#imperative-evaluations-evaluationlogger).

# Integrations overview

> Trace agents and LLM applications with Weave's integrations for agent SDKs, harnesses, LLM providers, and orchestration frameworks.

Weave provides two ways to integrate with your AI stack:

* **Trace agents**: for multi-turn agentic applications built with agent SDKs (such as the OpenAI Agents SDK or Google ADK) or run inside agent harnesses (such as Claude Code, Codex, or Pi.dev). These integrations capture sessions, turns, LLM calls, and tool calls, and render them in the Weave **Agents** view.
* **Trace LLM applications**: for code that calls LLM providers (OpenAI, Anthropic, Bedrock, and others) or uses orchestration frameworks (LangChain, LlamaIndex, DSPy, and others). These integrations capture individual LLM calls and pipeline steps as Weave **Calls** in the **Traces** view.

If you're not sure which path to take, start with [Trace your agents](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/tracking/trace-agents.md) for new multi-turn agent work, or [Trace LLM applications](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/tracking/tracing.md) for existing LLM-call workflows.

# Trace your agents

> Use the Weave SDK to instrument multi-turn agentic applications and view them in the Agents tab.

> [!TIP]
>
> **This workflow is also available in CoreWeave Agent Lens.** Agent Lens is the Forge experience built for tracing, monitoring, and analyzing AI agents, with automated insights into agent failures and user intents. It uses the same trace data as Weights & Biases Weave, so the traces you already send appear there with nothing to migrate.
> [See how to do this in Agent Lens](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/agent-lens/tracing/instrument.md).

Learn how to instrument a multi-turn agentic application using the W\&B Weave SDK so that you can view, debug, and evaluate your agent's behavior. This guide is intended for developers who build or integrate agents and want structured visibility into conversations, turns, LLM calls, and tool executions.

The Weave SDK for Agents models the full lifecycle of a multi-turn agent conversation: the agent that owns many conversations, the conversation that groups turns together, each user-agent exchange (turn), the LLM calls within a turn, and the tool executions that an LLM triggers. Traces appear in the **Agents** tab of your Weave project. Each conversation shows a multi-turn timeline with nested tool calls, token usage, and feedback.

Weave is built on [OpenTelemetry (OTel)](https://opentelemetry.io/docs/concepts/), the open standard for distributed tracing. Every turn, LLM call, and tool call emits an OTel *span* (a structured record of one operation). Each span is tagged with [GenAI semantic-convention](https://opentelemetry.io/docs/specs/semconv/gen-ai/) attributes like `gen_ai.agent.name` and `gen_ai.conversation.id`.

If you're tracing individual functions as Ops with the `@weave.op` decorator, see [Trace LLM applications](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/tracking/tracing.md) instead.

result.text:
## Traces

Traces are full trees of Calls that share the same execution context. Each Trace contains an ID (`trace_id`) you can use to retrieve the entire tree of Calls. If you retrieve Call information using the Call's ID, Weave returns data about the specified Call only, and none of its child Calls.

In short: tracing records what your application or agent did. Evaluations measure your application against a fixed, curated set of test cases. Signals score and tag the traced conversations of your live agents. The last two both rely on getting your app's activity into Weave.

**Tracing: records what happened**
- If you build agents with the Weave SDK for Agents, Weave records conversations, turns, LLM calls and tool calls as structured records called spans. You can view them in the **Agents** tab [S6]. The stated purpose is to let you "view, debug, and evaluate" your agent's behaviour [S6].
- For non-agent LLM code, integrations record individual calls as Weave **Calls** in the **Traces** view [S3]. A Trace is a full tree of Calls that share the same execution context [S7].

**Evaluations: testing before you ship**
- An `Evaluation` brings together a dataset of test examples and one or more scoring functions [S2].
- You run it against a `Model` or a function containing your app's logic. Each `.evaluate()` creates an evaluation run [S2]. In TypeScript, the target is any function wrapped with `weave.op` [S2].
- Use evaluations to compare changes over time and catch regressions [S2].

**Signals: monitoring agents in production**
- In the Agents view, the Signals tab shows tags and ratings for your agent's conversations [S1].
- A rating is a score between 0.0 and 1.0, and a tag is a label such as "user-frustration". Both are attached to matching spans [S4].
- Signals point out quality and safety problems and highlight the traces that need your attention [S1].

**How they fit together**
- Tracing is the foundation. Evaluations check changes against repeatable test cases [S2]. Signals keep scoring real agent conversations in production [S1].
- Putting these premises together: a Signal can flag a weak trace, and that can guide what you test next in an evaluation. The pages I read don't describe this as an official workflow.
- Note: Signals belong to the newer Agents workflow. They replace the older Monitors approach, so don't mix the two.

## View a linked run in the Traces table

When you call a function decorated with `@weave.op` inside a `wandb.init()` context of your ML pipeline, Weave automatically associates the trace with the active [Weights & Biases run](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/runs.md). The **Traces** table in the Weave UI links each trace to its associated runs.

To view the runs linked to your traces:

1. Run a script that calls traced functions inside a `wandb.init()` context, such as the training example in [Use Weave panels](#use-weave-panels).
2. Open the [Weights & Biases UI](https://forge.coreweave.com/wandb) and select your project.
3. In the **Weave** project sidebar, click **Traces**. The **Traces** table displays links to any associated runs.
4. Open a trace from the **Traces** table to inspect the linked run and review its experiment context.

> [!NOTE]
>
> The Weave TypeScript SDK doesn't support linking traces to Weights & Biases runs.

## What gets traced

After you run an agent with the exporter enabled, Koog forwards traces to your Weave project. Koog's Weave exporter captures the same spans as Koog's general OTEL integration, including:

* Agent lifecycle events (start, stop, errors)
* LLM interactions (prompts, completions, token usage, latency)
* Tool and API calls (function calls and external requests)
* System context (model name, Koog version, environment metadata)

You can visualize these traces in the Weights & Biases UI to understand performance and quality. See [Weave's tracing overview](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/tracking/tracing.md) for an introduction to capturing traces with Weave.

# Create and manage saved views

> Customize how you interact with traced function calls and evaluations

In Weave, *saved views* let you customize how you interact with traced function calls and evaluations. By defining a saved view, you can configure filters, sorting, and column visibility to quickly access relevant data. Saved views help you and your team return to the same curated slice of your traces or evaluations without reapplying configuration each time.

You can create, modify, and save views through the UI or directly in the Weave Python SDK. The UI lets you explore and save different table configurations in the **Traces** and **Evals** tabs, while the Python SDK provides fine-grained control for programmatic filtering and querying. Select the tab that matches your workflow.

**UI**

You can create, load, rename, and edit saved views in the Weights & Biases UI. The UI is the quickest way to capture an ad hoc table configuration as a reusable view. For programmatic control, select the **Python** tab.

result.text:
# Monitor using built-in signals

> Weights & Biases provides built-in scoring solutions for agents in production

> [!NOTE]
>
> This page covers a previous approach to monitoring production traffic. For new implementations, use **Signals** under Weave for Agents. See [View agent signals](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/tracking/view-agent-signals.md).

Standard system metrics like latency, token count, and cost don't fully capture agent behavior. Inspecting individual traces provides deep insight but doesn't scale to the millions of traces generated in a live environment.

Signals provide a high-level monitoring solution to this problem by offering automated, behavioral scoring for agents in production:

* Automated scoring: Every incoming production trace is automatically processed and scored on common quality issues and errors.
* Infrastructure: Processing is powered by CoreWeave compute and CoreWeave GPUs for scalability across millions of traces.

By using signals within production, you can:

* Gain behavioral insight. Move beyond system metrics to understand if your agent is hallucinating, failing to follow conversation patterns, or losing grounding in its evidence.
* Accelerate the research loop. Use the scores and failure analyses generated by signals to identify weaknesses, which you can use to research model improvement, data annotation, or reinforcement learning.
